hints: Notice the stem asks which description of an equal-magnitude Newton third law pair is not correct.
Recall that a third law pair comes from a single interaction, so check direction, whether the forces share one object or two, and whether the force type stays the same.
Compare with equilibrium, which requires two balanced forces acting on the same object, and decide if forces on different objects can do that.
walkthrough: Identify the test: the stem describes two equal-magnitude forces forming a Newton third law pair and asks for the false statement.
State the third law rule: if object X exerts a force on object Y, then object Y exerts an equal, opposite force of the same type back on object X.
Check opposite directions and different objects: both are required because the interaction is mutual between two objects along the same line.
Check same type of force: both arise from the same interaction, for example Earth pulls book down gravitationally and book pulls Earth up gravitationally.
Contrast with equilibrium: equilibrium needs resultant force zero on one object, but the pair never acts together on one object, so it cannot cause equilibrium. This is option D.

options.A: A Newton third law pair is equal, opposite and along the same line, so opposite directions is correct.
options.B: The two forces come from one interaction between two objects, so each force acts on a different object.
options.C: Both forces have the same origin, for example both gravitational or both contact forces, so same type is correct.
options.D: Equilibrium needs balanced forces on the same object, but a third law pair acts on different objects so it cannot balance one object.
